# What we are doing

We generate random data many times and see what happens. This is called a
Monte Carlo simulation.

1. Make Q-Q plots to see how normal data can look different just by chance.
2. Run a randomness test on 10,000 independent samples and count false alarms.
3. Fit a straight line, test the leftover errors, and compare the false alarms.

# Preparing the workspace

We only need two extra packages: `ggplot2` for the plots and `TSA` for the
runs test. The other functions come with R.

```{r packages}
# Install these packages only if they are missing.
listPackages <- c("ggplot2", "TSA")
for (package in listPackages) {
  if (!requireNamespace(package, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(package, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
}
library(ggplot2)
library(TSA)
```

# Part 1: Q-Q plots

## One sample

Generate 72 independent values from a normal distribution with mean 0 and
standard deviation 1. Standardizing means subtracting the sample mean and
dividing by the sample standard deviation.

```{r singleQQ}
set.seed(1943)
n <- 72
x <- rnorm(n)
z <- (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)

qqnorm(z)
abline(0, 1, col = "blue")
qqline(z, col = "red")
```

The blue line is $y=x$. The red line is fitted using the sample's first and
third quartiles. Points near a straight line are consistent with normal data.
Even genuinely normal samples do not fall exactly on a straight line.

## Several sets of six plots, with and without standardizing

The function below just saves us from copying the same plotting code six
times. It follows the plotting code in the tutorial. In these panels,
**red is $y=x$ and blue is the quartile line** (the same colours as the
tutorial's six-panel example).

```{r plot-function}
plot_six <- function(x, plot_title) {
  # Each column of x is one sample.
  d <- data.frame(
    value = as.vector(x),
    sample = factor(rep(1:6, each = nrow(x)))
  )

  ggplot(d, aes(sample = value)) +
    stat_qq(size = 0.5) +
    stat_qq_line(color = "blue") +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "red") +
    facet_wrap(~ sample, nrow = 3, ncol = 2) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = c(-3, 3), ylim = c(-4.5, 4.5)) +
    labs(title = plot_title,
         subtitle = "Red: y = x; Blue: quartile line",
         x = "Normal Quantiles", y = "Observed Quantiles") +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(panel.spacing = grid::unit(0, "pt"),
          panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA))
}
```

We set the seed once before the loop. Each round generates six new samples.
Within each round, we use the same samples before and after standardizing,
so the comparison is easier. `scale()` standardizes each column separately.

```{r repeatedQQ, fig.width=6, fig.height=9}
set.seed(123)
n <- 72

for (round in 1:3) {
  x <- matrix(rnorm(6 * n), nrow = n, ncol = 6)

  z <- scale(x)
  print(plot_six(z, paste("Standardized samples - set", round)))

  # This version does not use scale().
  print(plot_six(x, paste("Unstandardized samples - set", round)))
}
```

**Comments:** After standardizing, each sample has mean 0 and standard
deviation 1, so the $y=x$ line is a useful overall reference. The quartile
line can follow the middle points better, but it can also tilt away from
the tails. Neither line has to be closer to every point in every sample.

Without standardizing, the sample mean and standard deviation vary from
sample to sample. The quartile line can adjust its position and slope, so
it will often track the sample better than the fixed $y=x$ line.

The main lesson is that normal samples can have bends, gaps, and points
away from the line, especially at the ends. A few unusual-looking points
are not enough on their own to conclude that the data are non-normal.

# Part 2: The runs test on white noise

White noise here means independent normal values with mean 0 and constant
variance. A run is a consecutive group on the same side of a cutoff. For
example, `+++ -- +` has three runs. Too many or too few runs can suggest
that the ordering is not random.

```{r part2}
M <- 10000
n <- 72
set.seed(1943)

# Each column is one independent sample of 72 observations.
e <- matrix(rnorm(n * M), nrow = n)
pv_noise <- apply(e, 2, function(x) { TSA::runs(x)$pvalue })
length(unique(pv_noise))

qqplot(qunif(ppoints(M)), pv_noise, pch = 19, cex = 0.2,
       xlab = "Uniform Quantiles", ylab = "Runs-test p-values",
       main = "White noise")
abline(0, 1, col = "blue")
```

**Explaining the two requested lines:**

- `apply(e, 2, ...)` takes one column of `e` at a time. The `2` means columns.
  Each column is passed to the function as `x`.
- `TSA::runs(x)` applies the runs test, and `$pvalue` extracts its p-value.
  `pv_noise` stores all 10,000 p-values. It is the tutorial's `pv` variable,
  renamed so that Part 3 does not overwrite it.
- `unique(pv_noise)` keeps each distinct p-value once. `length(...)` counts
  how many distinct p-values there are.

The Q-Q plot compares these p-values with a uniform distribution from 0
to 1. Ideally calibrated continuous p-values would follow the diagonal.
Here, the runs statistic is discrete, so repeated p-values and steps are
expected; the plot need not be perfectly straight.

## Counts and estimated Type I error

**Correction to the wording in the tutorial:** p-values *larger* than
0.05 correspond to not rejecting. A Type I error means rejecting a true
null hypothesis, so we count p-values **less than or equal to 0.05**.
We show both counts below.

```{r noise-counts}
above_noise <- sum(pv_noise > 0.05)
reject_noise <- sum(pv_noise <= 0.05)
rate_noise <- reject_noise / M

above_noise
reject_noise
rate_noise
```

There are **`r above_noise`** p-values above 0.05 and
**`r reject_noise`** p-values at or below 0.05.
The estimated Type I error probability is **`r round(rate_noise, 4)`**,
or **`r round(100 * rate_noise, 2)`%**. These are false alarms because
the samples really are independent white noise.

## A 95% confidence interval

Each simulation either rejects or does not reject. This lets us use a
binomial confidence interval for the true rejection probability.

```{r noise-ci}
ci_noise <- binom.test(reject_noise, M, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
inside_noise <- ci_noise[1] <= 0.05 && 0.05 <= ci_noise[2]
ci_noise
inside_noise

# Use the interval to allow for Monte Carlo uncertainty.
if (ci_noise[2] < 0.05) {
  conclusion_noise <- "conservative"
} else if (ci_noise[1] > 0.05) {
  conclusion_noise <- "liberal"
} else {
  conclusion_noise <- "consistent with being well calibrated at 5%"
}
```

The 95% interval is
**(`r round(ci_noise[1], 4)`, `r round(ci_noise[2], 4)`)**.
Is 0.05 inside? **`r if (inside_noise) "Yes" else "No"`.**
The simulation suggests that the test is **`r conclusion_noise`**.
Conservative means fewer false alarms than 5%; liberal means more than 5%.
An interval containing 0.05 is compatible with 5%, but does not prove the
true probability is exactly 0.05.

# Part 3: The runs test on regression residuals

A residual is the observed value minus the value predicted by a fitted
line. We keep the matrix code supplied in the tutorial. It removes a
fitted intercept and slope from each sample all at once.

```{r part3}
M <- 10000
n <- 72

# First column: intercept. Second column: fixed predictor values.
desmat <- cbind(rep(1, n), qnorm(ppoints(n)))
hatmat <- desmat %*% solve(t(desmat) %*% desmat, t(desmat))
id.minus.hatmat <- diag(n) - hatmat
sum(diag(hatmat))

set.seed(1943)
e <- matrix(rnorm(n * M), nrow = n)

# Subtract the fitted line from each sample to obtain residuals.
res <- id.minus.hatmat %*% e
pv_res <- apply(res, 2, function(x) { TSA::runs(x)$pvalue })

length(unique(pv_res))
qqplot(qunif(ppoints(M)), pv_res, pch = 19, cex = 0.2,
       xlab = "Uniform Quantiles", ylab = "Runs-test p-values",
       main = "Regression residuals")
abline(0, 1, col = "blue")
```

`hatmat` produces fitted values. `diag(n)` is the identity matrix, so
`id.minus.hatmat` subtracts the fitted values from the original data.
The diagonal sum is 2 because the regression estimates two parameters:
an intercept and a slope.

We do not need to add a nonzero trend before finding residuals: fitting
the same intercept and slope would remove that trend anyway.

## Counts, summary, and conclusion

```{r residual-results}
reject_res <- sum(pv_res <= 0.05)
rate_res <- reject_res / M
reject_res
summary(pv_res)
rate_res

ci_res <- binom.test(reject_res, M, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
inside_res <- ci_res[1] <= 0.05 && 0.05 <= ci_res[2]
ci_res
inside_res

if (ci_res[2] < 0.05) {
  conclusion_res <- "conservative relative to the nominal 5% rate"
} else if (ci_res[1] > 0.05) {
  conclusion_res <- "liberal relative to the nominal 5% rate"
} else {
  conclusion_res <- "consistent with a rejection rate of 5%"
}
```

For residuals, **`r reject_res`** out of 10,000 samples reject.
The estimated rejection probability is **`r round(rate_res, 4)`**
(**`r round(100 * rate_res, 2)`%**).
The 95% interval is **(`r round(ci_res[1], 4)`, `r round(ci_res[2], 4)`)**.
Is 0.05 inside? **`r if (inside_res) "Yes" else "No"`.**
The test is **`r conclusion_res`** in this simulation.

Unlike the original errors, residuals within a sample are not independent:
they share the same fitted line and must sum to zero. Therefore, this is a
rejection rate under the fitted regression model, rather than an exact
Type I error rate under independent observations. The separate simulated
samples are still independent, so the binomial interval remains suitable
for estimating this rejection rate.

```{r comparison}
comparison <- data.frame(
  Data = c("White noise", "Regression residuals"),
  Rejections = c(reject_noise, reject_res),
  Rate = c(rate_noise, rate_res),
  CI_lower = c(ci_noise[1], ci_res[1]),
  CI_upper = c(ci_noise[2], ci_res[2])
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4)
```
